analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the individual income tax cuts that were set to expire after 2025.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced January 29, 2018 with 75 Republican cosponsors and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, it stayed there until the 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) cut individual income tax rates, roughly doubled the standard deduction, expanded the child tax credit, reduced the alternative minimum tax, and created a 20% deduction for owners of pass-through businesses. To comply with Senate budget rules, most of those individual provisions were written to expire after 2025. This bill would have struck that expiration date, making the individual tax cuts permanent instead of letting them lapse.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that pay income tax would keep lower rates and a larger standard deduction indefinitely. In dollar terms, the largest gains go to the highest earners and to owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, S-corps, and sole proprietorships like law firms, medical practices, and real estate holdings), who benefit from the top-rate cut, AMT relief, and the 20% pass-through deduction. Middle-income families also keep real, smaller cuts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and business owners, plus middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Keeps the individual income tax rate cuts, doubled standard deduction, and expanded child tax credit in place past their scheduled 2025 expiration.
Makes permanent the reduced alternative minimum tax, which mainly benefits higher-income filers, and the individual-side provisions of the 2017 law generally.
Locks in the 20% deduction for pass-through business income, which flows disproportionately to business owners rather than wage earners.
The bill's own 'sense of Congress' states the sunsets existed only because Senate budget reconciliation rules forced them, and argues for acting immediately to give taxpayers certainty.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Because the 2017 cuts were not paid for, making them permanent would add to deficits for as far as projections run, which eventually forces some combination of higher future taxes, lower federal spending, or more borrowing whose interest costs fall on everyone.

drawbacks.text: Making the sunsets disappear would forgo hundreds of billions of dollars of revenue over ten years, deepening deficits that were already projected to grow; the bill contained no offsetting revenue.

The dollar value of the individual cuts is concentrated at the top: top-bracket rate relief, AMT repeal, and the pass-through deduction are worth the most to high earners, while a lapse in 2025 would have been an opportunity to re-balance the code.

The 2025 sunset was not an accident; it was the mechanism that let the 2017 law pass with a 10-year budget window, so erasing it removes the built-in future chance to reassess the law's cost and distribution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Real tax cuts for many ordinary families are on the plus side of the ledger, and they are popular. But the design is lopsided: the biggest dollar benefits go to the highest earners and business owners, and the bill made no attempt to pay for permanence, meaning the cost would surface later as deficits, spending pressure, or future tax increases. An honest version aimed at ordinary workers would have made the middle-class pieces permanent while letting the provisions that skew to the top lapse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee on January 29, 2018, and the committee never took it up before the 115th Congress ended, so it expired with no markup and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Rodney Davis of Illinois introduced the bill on January 29, 2018, with 43 original cosponsors signing on at introduction.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which held jurisdiction over tax legislation.
Seventy-five House Republicans eventually cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill would have removed the December 31, 2025 expiration date from the individual-tax and AMT provisions of the 2017 tax law.
The bill's own text acknowledges the sunsets were required by the Senate budget reconciliation process rather than chosen on the merits.
No further action was recorded after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, several hundred billion dollars of unpaid-for revenue was not committed to permanence, and the question of which 2017 tax cuts to extend was left to a later Congress with full budget information. Taxpayers who expected the cuts to expire also lost the certainty the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue and the 2025 tax debate

for.name: Rep. Rodney Davis
for.role: House Republican from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 29, 2018 and recruited 43 original cosponsors.

for.name: 75 of 240 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, signing on entirely within the Republican conference.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote in the eleven months after referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor despite unanimous Republican cosponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: All 75 cosponsors were House Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the committee and floor inaction came from the Republican majority itself.

industries.note: The bill permanently extends the 20% deduction on pass-through income, a break whose dollar benefits concentrate among owners of partnerships, S-corps, law firms, medical practices, and real estate holdings rather than salaried workers. Making it permanent removes the 2025 chance to restructure or means-test it.

Permanent top-rate cuts and permanent AMT relief are worth the most in dollars to filers at the top of the income distribution. Their gain comes at the cost of the revenue that funds public services or that would otherwise reduce deficits.

Households at middle incomes keep a larger standard deduction, the expanded child tax credit, and lower rates indefinitely, which is a genuine and popular benefit, though smaller in dollar terms than what accrues at the top.
Foregone revenue from permanent cuts would widen deficits, putting pressure on future Congresses to cut spending, raise other taxes, or carry more interest costs.
